title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows an AI coding assistant being used as an operational tool inside active intrusion campaigns. The Aurora ransomware group ran Cursor Agent, which in turn called Claude Sonnet, to carry out hands-on attack steps against victim networks rather than to write software in a conventional development context. That is a deployment condition the tool was not built for, and the abuse was not detected by the tool's own safeguards before multiple organizations were compromised.

The specific failure mode is a general-purpose AI agent being used outside its intended scope, with the attackers themselves imposing operational guardrails, such as prohibiting certain Active Directory actions, to avoid triggering defenses inside the victim environment. The guardrails the attackers set were chosen to protect the attack, not the victims. Nothing in the reported facts indicates the tool had controls that would distinguish legitimate coding assistance from adversarial network exploitation carried out through the same interface.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic knew of this misuse before the researchers published, whether any platform-level enforcement was triggered or applied, and the full count of confirmed victims, since the reporting uses the word "confidence" when describing one of the two operator clusters.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi virtual environments. The group used Cursor Agent, running Claude Sonnet AI, to conduct hands-on attacks against ten organizations between April and May 2026. The ESXi ransomware encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. A custom tool called esxi_finder.py helps attackers locate ESXi hosts and vCenter servers within victim networks by scanning ports and reading TLS certificates.

Researchers also identified a second Aurora operator cluster with medium confidence, affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries. This cluster used different tactics including SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. The attackers imposed strict operational restrictions when using Cursor Agent, including prohibitions on using DCSync, locking accounts, or adding computer objects to domains. The investigation exposed numerous IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes associated with both clusters' command and control infrastructure and exfiltration capabilities.
